newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon army says attacks aimed at ties with Syria.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon army says attacks aimed at ties with Syria.

text.p: The Lebanese army said on Tuesday a recent wave of attacks inside the country was aimed at wrecking Lebanon's close ties with Syria and served only the interests of Israel.
Army commander General Emile Lahoud acknowledged that his soldiers had taken part in a detention campaign over the past week but said the arrests were made in line with the law.
International human rights and press freedom organisations have blasted the arrests as illegal and urged Beirut to free the detainees.

"All the duties carried out by the army including breaking into (the homes of suspects) and the detentions are based on the principles of law, rights and duties and follow the instructions of the judicial authorities," Lahoud said.

It was the army's first comment on the wave of arrests sparked by an incident last week in which a van carrying Syrian workers was machine-gunned in a predominantly Christian area, killing the driver and injuring some passengers.

"Some recent activities that disturbed internal security were aimed at serving the enemy (Israel) at the expense of national stabiltiy and aimed at wrecking the Syrian-Lebanese unity in the face of regional challenges," Lahoud told soldiers during a visit to south Lebanon frontlines with Israeli occupation forces.

Israel's five-year-old peace talks with Lebanon and Syria have been stalled over the issue of Israeli troop withdrawal from occupied Arab land. Some 1,000 Israeli troops hold a 15-km (nine mile)-wide south Lebanon border zone.

"During this critical phase in the history of the region we regard as equals those who destabilise internal security and the Israeli enemy in the south. We consider those who serve the interests of the enemy as an extension to this enemy," Lahoud said.
With 35,000 troops deployed across Lebanon, Damascus is Lebanon's main power broker and the two countries closely coordinate all peace moves with Israel.
Lebanese Prosecutor-General Adnan Addoum said on Monday that out of 48 detained people 26 had been freed. He said none of the detainees had been charged with any offences.
Lebanese Christian opposition politicians at home and in Paris put the number of detainees at 200.
The latest person known to have been held was Christian journalist Pierre Atallah of the Beirut conservative An-Nahar newspaper.
Atallah was detained by "the Lebanese army and army intelligence" on Monday night, Joubran Tweini, one of the owners of An-Nahar, told Reuters.
When asked to comment on the report, a senior security official said "all detentions are of a security nature and not related to the freedom of expression".

Tweini said: "Pierre was kidnapped, not detained. The two men who came after him, an army officer and an army intelligence agent, refused to show him any arrest warrant. They pointed their guns at his head and took him to an unknown place.
A Paris-based international human rights watchdog, The International Federation of Human Rights Leagues, accused Lebanon on Tuesday of torturing detainees.
The group said it had good reasons to believe most if not all detainees "are now being tortured".
It listed the names of 26 individuals it said had been detained in the past week without arrest warrants by individuals in civilian clothing.
